before.content_html:
Pure Substances and Mixtures

In chemistry, a pure substance consists of a single element or compound. A pure substance melts and boils at a precise, fixed temperature. A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically bonded together. Mixtures melt and boil over a range of temperatures, not at a fixed point — and this difference is the basis of purity testing.

To test whether a sample is pure, measure its melting point and compare it to the accepted value for that substance. If the melting point is lower than expected and occurs over a range of temperatures, the sample contains impurities. This technique is used routinely in pharmaceutical quality control to check that a medicine contains the correct active compound.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp melting point at a fixed temperature. A mixture melts over a range of temperatures. Impurities lower the melting point and broaden the melting range.

Separation Techniques

Because mixtures are not chemically combined, their components can be separated using physical methods. The correct technique depends on the nature of the mixture and the properties of its components.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel; the solid remains as the residue and the liquid passes through as the filtrate. For example, sand is separated from salt solution by filtration.

Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid from solution. The solution is heated to evaporate most of the solvent, then left to cool slowly. As the solution cools, the dissolved substance becomes less soluble and forms crystals. The crystals can be filtered and dried. This is used to purify soluble salts such as copper sulfate.

Simple distillation works when the substances in a mixture have very different boiling points (usually more than 25°C apart). The mixture is heated; the more volatile liquid evaporates first, the vapour is cooled in a condenser, and the liquid is collected. For example, distilled water is produced from salt solution by simple distillation — water evaporates and is condensed, leaving salts behind.

Fractional distillation is used when liquids have similar boiling points. A fractionating column is packed with glass beads or plates that provide surfaces for condensation. Liquids with lower boiling points travel further up the column and are collected first. This is the method used to separate crude oil into fractions such as petrol, kerosene, and diesel.

Chromatography

Chromatography separates substances in a mixture based on how strongly they are attracted to the stationary phase (e.g. paper) compared to how soluble they are in the moving phase (the solvent). In paper chromatography, a pencil line is drawn near the bottom of the paper, spots of mixture are placed on the line, and the paper is placed in solvent. As the solvent moves up, it carries substances with it — those that are more soluble travel further.

The position of each spot is described by its Rf value:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$

Each substance has a unique Rf value in a given solvent at a given temperature. A pure substance gives a single spot; a mixture gives multiple spots at different heights. By comparing Rf values with reference values, or by running known substances alongside the unknown, substances can be identified.

Key Fact

Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent. In a given solvent, each substance has a unique Rf value. A pure substance produces one spot; a mixture produces multiple spots.

To carry out a paper chromatography investigation: draw a pencil baseline (not pen — ink would also travel) near the bottom of the chromatography paper. Spot the sample mixture and reference substances on the baseline. Place the paper in a small amount of appropriate solvent — the solvent level must be below the pencil line so the spots do not dissolve directly into the solvent pot. Allow the solvent to rise until it nears the top of the paper, then remove and immediately mark the solvent front with pencil. Measure distances from the pencil line to calculate Rf values. Variables to control include the type of solvent and the length of time the chromatogram is run.

Instrumental Methods of Identification

As well as chromatography, modern laboratories use instrumental techniques that are faster, more sensitive, and capable of analysing very small samples. Mass spectrometry identifies compounds by fragmenting molecules into ions and measuring their mass-to-charge ratios. The output is a mass spectrum: a graph showing the relative abundance of different fragment masses. The largest fragment (the molecular ion) gives the relative molecular mass of the compound. Mass spectrometry is used in forensic science, drug testing, and quality control of pharmaceuticals.

Flame tests use the colour of light emitted when a compound is heated in a flame to identify metal ions. Lithium gives a crimson flame; sodium gives yellow; potassium gives lilac; calcium gives red-orange; copper gives blue-green. These are qualitative tests — they tell you which metal is present but not how much.
before.exam_tip_html: For the required practical chromatography question, always state why a pencil baseline is used (pen ink would travel in the solvent). When asked to calculate an Rf value, make sure you measure from the baseline to the centre of each spot, not from the bottom of the paper. If asked about purity, always link melting point evidence to the conclusion — a melting range rather than a sharp point indicates a mixture.

practice_questions.text: A student tests the melting point of a white powder. The powder starts to melt at 48°C and is fully melted by 57°C. The accepted melting point of the pure compound is 52°C. What can the student conclude about the purity of the powder?

Secure: states impure with reference to melting range. Developing: states impure but explanation is weak. Emerging: no link between evidence and conclusion.

practice_questions.text: A student runs paper chromatography on a food dye sample. The solvent front travels 9.0 cm. Spot A travels 6.3 cm. Calculate the Rf value of spot A and identify whether spot A could be the same substance as a reference compound with Rf = 0.70.
practice_questions.marks: Rf = 6.3 ÷ 9.0 = 0.70 (1 mark for correct calculation); yes, spot A could be the same substance as the reference compound because their Rf values are equal (1 mark). Mastering: correct calculation and reasoned comparison. Secure: correct answer. Developing: correct formula used but arithmetic error. Emerging: formula not recalled.

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper chromatography could be used to determine whether a sample of green food colouring contains more than one dye. Include the key steps and how you would interpret the result.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: spot sample on pencil baseline on chromatography paper; place in solvent below the baseline; allow solvent to rise (1); remove and mark solvent front with pencil; calculate Rf values (1); if multiple spots appear at different heights, the colouring contains more than one dye; a pure dye would give a single spot (1). Secure: three steps described. Developing: two steps with partial interpretation. Emerging: one step.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fractional distillation rather than simple distillation is used to separate the components of crude oil.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: crude oil contains many components with similar boiling points (1); simple distillation cannot separate liquids with close boiling points as they evaporate at similar temperatures (1); the fractionating column allows repeated condensation and evaporation, progressively separating liquids by boiling point into fractions (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: mentions different boiling points without explaining how separation works.

practice_questions.text: A crime scene analyst uses mass spectrometry to identify an unknown white powder. Explain how mass spectrometry works and why it is preferred over a melting point test in this context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: mass spectrometry ionises molecules and measures mass-to-charge ratios of fragments (1); the molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass (1); mass spectrometry can identify substances from very small samples with high sensitivity (1); a melting point test only works if you know what you expect and have enough material to observe a clear melting range (1); in forensic work where the identity is unknown, mass spectrometry identifies without prior knowledge and can detect trace amounts (1). Secure: 3–4 points. Developing: 2 points. Emerging: 1 point.

practice_questions.text: Outline a method to obtain pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from a mixture of copper sulfate dissolved in water.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: heat the copper sulfate solution to evaporate most of the water (1); remove from heat and leave to cool slowly — crystals form as solubility decreases (1); filter the crystals to separate them from the remaining solution (residue on filter paper, filtrate discarded) (1); dry the crystals gently, e.g. by leaving on filter paper in a warm place or a low oven (1). Secure: all four steps. Developing: three steps. Emerging: one or two steps.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points; mixtures melt over a range. Purity testing compares the measured melting point against the accepted value.
  • Separation techniques (filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation) are chosen based on the properties of the components; chromatography separates and identifies dissolved substances by their Rf values in a given solvent.
  • Instrumental methods such as mass spectrometry can identify substances with greater speed and sensitivity than traditional tests, and are widely used in forensic science and pharmaceutical quality control.

before.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (\ (H^+\)) in water. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a soluble base — it produces hydroxide ions (\ (OH^-\)) in solution. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis (some bases are insoluble, such as copper oxide).

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline. pH is measured using universal indicator (colour matched to a chart) or a digital pH probe (more precise). The scale is logarithmic — each unit change represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in water; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\). pH 0–6 = acidic; 7 = neutral; 8–14 = alkaline.

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base. The general ionic equation is:

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$$

The products are a salt and water. The key reactions of acids that produce salts are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. E.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

Naming Salts and Making Them

A salt takes its name from the metal and the acid. Hydrochloric acid (\ (HCl\)) produces chlorides; sulfuric acid (\ (H_2SO_4\)) produces sulfates; nitric acid (\ (HNO_3\)) produces nitrates. To predict a salt, name the metal first, then the acid type — e.g. zinc + hydrochloric acid gives zinc chloride.

To prepare a pure, dry salt: add an excess of insoluble base (e.g. copper oxide) to a warm acid (e.g. sulfuric acid) and stir. The excess solid ensures all acid is used up. Filter off the unreacted solid. Gently heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, then leave to cool so crystals form. Filter the crystals and dry at low temperature. The excess base guarantees no acid remains in the product — this is the key step that distinguishes this method from a titration.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. Predict any salt: metal name + acid type. Example: magnesium + nitric acid = magnesium nitrate.

Titration

Titration is used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali (or vice versa). The method uses a burette to deliver acid accurately, a pipette to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask, and an indicator to detect the end point (when the solution changes colour, showing neutralisation is complete).

Set up a burette filled with acid and record the initial reading. Using a pipette and filler, transfer a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask. Add two or three drops of indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange). Slowly add acid from the burette, swirling the flask. Add dropwise near the end point — the indicator will change colour permanently when neutralisation is complete. Record the final burette reading. The titre is the volume of acid added (final reading minus initial reading). Repeat until two concordant results are obtained (within 0.10 cm3 of each other). Average the concordant titres for accuracy.

Strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric) fully ionise in water — every molecule releases its \(H^+\) ions. Weak acids (ethanoic, citric) only partially ionise, establishing an equilibrium. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid because it produces more \(H^+\) ions. Concentration and strength are different properties — a dilute strong acid can have the same pH as a concentrated weak acid.

Indicators and Measuring pH

An indicator is a substance whose colour depends on pH. Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that shows a range of colours: red and orange for strongly acidic solutions, green for neutral, blue and violet for alkaline solutions. However, it gives only an approximate pH reading. For more accurate measurement, a pH probe is used — these give a numerical reading to several decimal places and are essential in research and industry.

Phenolphthalein is a specific indicator that is colourless in acid and turns pink in alkali. Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and red in acid. The choice of indicator in a titration depends on the strength of the acid and alkali being used. For a strong acid reacting with a strong alkali, either indicator works well. The end point shows a permanent colour change that means exactly enough acid has been added to neutralise all the alkali.

Everyday Examples of Neutralisation

Neutralisation reactions are not just laboratory techniques — they are at work in agriculture, medicine, and industry. Farmers add powdered limestone (calcium carbonate) or quicklime (calcium oxide) to acidic soils to raise the pH, making conditions better for crops. Indigestion remedies work by neutralising excess stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) with a mild alkali such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate. Toothpastes often contain mild alkalis to neutralise the acids produced by bacteria in the mouth, which cause tooth decay. Understanding which acid is present and which base will neutralise it efficiently is a practical application of this chemistry.
before.exam_tip_html: In questions about making salts, a common error is not explaining why an excess of solid is added — always state it ensures all acid is neutralised. For titration questions, name the dependent variable (volume of acid added), the independent variable (concentration of alkali or acid being found), and the controlled variables (volume of alkali, indicator used, temperature). When asked about strong vs weak acids, do not confuse strength with concentration: a strong acid fully ionises; concentration refers to the amount of acid dissolved per litre.

before.content_html:
Rate of Reaction

The rate of reaction tells you how quickly a reaction proceeds. It is calculated from:

$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The units of rate depend on how the quantity is measured. If you measure the volume of gas produced in cm3 over time in seconds, the rate has units of cm3/s. A common student error is to measure volume in cm3 but record time in minutes, and then forget to convert — always check your units match.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction can be increased by: raising temperature, increasing concentration (or pressure for gases), increasing surface area of solid reactants, or using a catalyst. Rate = quantity of reactant or product ÷ time.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains why rate changes when conditions change. A reaction only occurs when particles: (1) collide with each other, and (2) have at least the activation energy. If either condition is not met, particles bounce off without reacting.

Each factor affects either the frequency of collisions or the proportion that have enough energy:

  • Temperature — raising temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion exceed the activation energy.
  • Concentration / Pressure — more particles in a given volume means more frequent collisions.
  • Surface area — breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface, increasing the area available for collisions.
  • Catalyst — provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. More collisions now have sufficient energy to succeed. The catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation.

Three common methods to measure reaction rate:

  1. Gas collection — gas produced is collected in a gas syringe or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder. Volume is recorded at intervals.
  2. Mass loss — the reaction vessel sits on a balance; mass decreases as gas escapes. Mass is recorded at intervals.
  3. Colour/turbidity change — used for reactions that produce a precipitate or change colour. The “disappearing cross” experiment (sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid) measures the time for a cross beneath the flask to become invisible as sulfur precipitate forms. Rate = 1 ÷ time.

A reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid produces CO2 gas. After 20 s, 30 cm3 of gas has been collected. After 40 s, 50 cm3. Calculate the mean rate between 20 s and 40 s.

Rate = change in volume ÷ change in time = (50 − 30) cm3 ÷ (40 − 20) s = 20 ÷ 20 = 1.0 cm3/s.

Note: the units are cm3/s because volume was measured in cm3 and time in seconds. If time had been measured in minutes, the rate would be 1.0 cm3/min — these are not the same value. Always match units before calculating.

Key Fact

Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway. More collisions have sufficient energy to succeed. The catalyst is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation.

Yield and Atom Economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained to what you could theoretically obtain:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Yield is rarely 100%. Reasons include: the reaction may not go to completion, some product is lost in filtering or transferring, or a reversible reaction may not fully favour the products. In industry, maximising yield while controlling costs is a key challenge.

Atom economy measures how efficiently atoms from reactants end up in the desired product:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{\text{relative formula mass of desired product}}{\text{sum of relative formula masses of all products}} \times 100$$

A high atom economy means less waste. Addition reactions (where all reactants become one product) have 100% atom economy. Reactions that produce by-products have lower atom economy. Green chemistry aims to maximise atom economy to reduce waste and cost.

Consider the reaction: \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\). The desired product is CaO (\(M_r = 56\)). The by-product is CO2 (\(M_r = 44\)). Total mass of products = 56 + 44 = 100. Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56%. This means 44% of the atom mass ends up as the waste gas CO2.

Why Yield and Rate Both Matter

In industry, the goal is not simply to achieve the fastest possible rate or the highest possible yield — it is to produce the most product economically over time. A reaction that runs very quickly but has a low yield may be less profitable than a slower reaction with a high yield, depending on the cost of raw materials and energy. Conversely, a reaction with a high theoretical yield but a very slow rate may not be commercially viable without a catalyst to speed it up.

Industrial chemists therefore optimise conditions to balance rate and yield together. For example, using a catalyst simultaneously increases rate (without reducing yield) while allowing lower temperatures — reducing energy costs. Recycling unreacted starting materials back into the reaction vessel can also improve the overall yield over time, even if the yield at any single pass is moderate. These economic and environmental factors make the design of industrial chemical processes genuinely complex, and they illustrate why chemistry has real-world importance beyond the laboratory.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rate of reaction = quantity of reactant or product ÷ time. Four factors increase rate: higher temperature, higher concentration (or pressure), greater surface area, or a catalyst — all explained by collision theory and the activation energy concept.
  • Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Yield is rarely 100% due to incomplete reactions, product loss, or reversible reactions.
  • Atom economy = (\(M_r\) of desired product ÷ total \(M_r\) of all products) × 100. High atom economy means less waste; addition reactions have 100% atom economy.

before.content_html:
Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium

Some reactions are reversible — the products can re-form the original reactants. Reversible reactions are shown with a double arrow (\ (\rightleftharpoons\)). A simple example is the thermal decomposition and reformation of ammonium chloride:

$$NH_4Cl \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + HCl$$

When heated, ammonium chloride decomposes; when cooled, the gases recombine. In a closed system (where nothing enters or leaves), a reversible reaction eventually reaches dynamic equilibrium. At this point:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal).
  • The reaction has not stopped — both directions are still occurring simultaneously.
Key Fact

Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant but not equal to each other. In a reversible reaction, if the forward direction is exothermic, the reverse is endothermic by exactly the same amount of energy.

Le Chatelier’s Principle

Le Chatelier’s principle predicts how equilibrium responds to changing conditions. If you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to counteract that change:

  • Temperature: increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (to absorb the extra heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • Concentration: increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products. Increasing product concentration shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Pressure (gases only): increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium position. It speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached more quickly but the yield at equilibrium is unchanged.

The Haber Process

The Haber process manufactures ammonia (\ (NH_3\)) on an industrial scale. Ammonia is the starting material for fertilisers, nitric acid, and many other chemicals. Without fertilisers, global food production could not support the current world population. The equation is:

$$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3 \quad \Delta H = \text{exothermic}$$

The raw materials are: nitrogen from fractional distillation of liquid air, and hydrogen from the reaction of natural gas (methane) with steam.

Key Fact

Haber process conditions: approximately 450°C, approximately 200 atmospheres pressure, iron catalyst. The equation is \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3\) (exothermic forward reaction). Unreacted gases are recycled.

Compromise Conditions — Why These Values?

The Haber process involves deliberate trade-offs between rate and yield. Understanding these trade-offs is the core of this lesson.

The forward reaction (making ammonia) is exothermic. By Le Chatelier’s principle, a lower temperature favours the exothermic forward direction and gives a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia. However, at low temperatures the rate of reaction is also very slow — it would take a very long time to produce economically useful amounts. A higher temperature increases rate but decreases yield. Around 450°C is a compromise: fast enough to be practical, but not so hot that the yield drops too low to be profitable.

The left side of the equation has 4 moles of gas (\ (N_2 + 3H_2\)) and the right side has 2 moles (\ (2NH_3\)). By Le Chatelier’s principle, higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas — the right side, producing more ammonia. In theory, the higher the pressure, the better the yield. However, very high pressures require expensive, reinforced equipment and are costly to maintain and dangerous to run. About 200 atmospheres is again a compromise: it gives a good yield without making the plant uneconomically expensive to build and operate.

An iron catalyst is used to speed up both the forward and reverse reactions, allowing equilibrium to be reached more quickly. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the yield — it only reduces the time needed to get there. Because the yield at equilibrium is around 15–25% under these conditions, the ammonia is continuously removed by cooling and condensing it to a liquid. The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back into the reaction vessel. Recycling ensures raw materials are not wasted and the overall yield of the process is much higher than the equilibrium yield suggests.

Why Ammonia Matters: Fertilisers

Most ammonia produced by the Haber process is converted into fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate. Nitrogen is an essential element for plant growth — it is needed to make amino acids, proteins, and DNA. Without synthetic fertilisers, crop yields would be far lower and food would be more expensive or scarce. However, if fertilisers wash off fields into rivers and lakes, they can cause eutrophication — excessive algal growth that depletes oxygen in the water, harming fish and other aquatic life.

The Haber Process as a Science-Society Decision

The Haber process is a compelling example of how industrial chemistry involves decisions that go beyond pure science. The compromise conditions chosen (temperature, pressure, catalyst) are not determined by the chemistry alone — they reflect the balance between what is chemically optimal and what is economically and technically feasible. Building and maintaining pressure vessels safe to operate at very high pressures is expensive. Running processes at very high temperatures consumes large amounts of energy, contributing to operating costs and carbon emissions.

Modern industrial ammonia production continues to evolve. Researchers are investigating lower-temperature, lower-pressure catalytic routes (sometimes called “green ammonia” pathways) that could reduce energy demands and allow ammonia synthesis to be powered by renewable electricity. This illustrates a recurring theme in applied science: the conditions chosen today are not necessarily permanent — they reflect the best available technology at a given time, and new evidence or new materials can change the picture. Evaluating these developments requires weighing evidence about cost, feasibility, and environmental impact together.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process uses a temperature of approximately 450°C. The forward reaction making ammonia is exothermic. Explain why a lower temperature would give a higher yield but is not used industrially.

Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: The equation for the Haber process is: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Explain why high pressure increases the yield of ammonia, and suggest why a pressure of approximately 200 atmospheres is chosen rather than a much higher pressure.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process. In your answer, state what the catalyst does and does not affect.

practice_questions.text: In the Haber process, the yield of ammonia at the operating conditions is moderate. Explain how the industrial process overcomes this limitation to produce ammonia economically.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the ammonia is continuously removed from the reaction vessel by cooling and condensing it to a liquid (1); removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium to the right to replace it, producing more ammonia (Le Chatelier) (1); unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled back into the reaction vessel (1); this means the raw materials are not wasted (1); over time, the overall yield of the process is much greater than the equilibrium yield suggests (1). Secure: 3–4 points. Developing: 2 points. Emerging: 1 point.

practice_questions.text: Ammonia produced by the Haber process is used to make nitrogen fertilisers. Explain one environmental problem that can arise from the use of nitrogen fertilisers on farmland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: nitrogen fertilisers can wash off fields into rivers or lakes in rain (1); this causes excessive algal growth (eutrophication) because algae use the extra nitrates as nutrients (1); the algae block light, and when they die, decomposing bacteria deplete oxygen in the water, harming or killing aquatic life (1).
